picks.style: greek hymn to the lyre, kithara over soft drone, single clear voice with chorus, spellbound, slow, hovering
picks.why: 'Golden lyre... you quench even the warlike thunderbolt' — the eagle asleep on Zeus's scepter, rippling his back to the music. The most beautiful opening in Pindar.

picks.style: greek gnomic ode, low lyre and hand drum, grave baritone, measured, cautionary, dark-toned
picks.why: Asclepius struck down for raising the dead, and then 'Do not crave immortal life, my soul, but use to the full the resources of what is possible.'

picks.style: greek civic ode, aulos and lyre with light percussion, chorus answering a soloist, ceremonial, poised, gathering
picks.why: 'Kindly Peace, daughter of Justice, holding the supreme keys of counsels and of wars' — an invocation that turns and sinks Arrogance in the flood.

picks.style: qawwali-tinged ghazal, harmonium, dholak and hand-claps, lead voice with chorus answering the refrain, insistent, building
picks.why: The radif 'in just a little while' lands on its own line every couplet — a hook already written, and the moth's ash on the ground to hang it on.

picks.style: urdu ghazal, harmonium and tabla, expressive male vocal, rubato, intimate, sardonic
picks.why: 'Those aren't two rows of lashes... one sweet disaster with its lovely twin contends' — and the world as an old brawler who has never once sought peace.

picks.style: delhi ghazal, sarangi and tabla, weathered male voice, slow, valedictory, aching in the turns
picks.why: 'In this world's inn, we came and then we went away' — plus the loosened hair turning every wave of the river into a black snake.

picks.style: latin tragic invocation, low drone with bowed strings and struck bronze, fierce female voice, slow, mounting, ritual
picks.why: Medea calling first on the marriage gods, then on chaos and the impious shades — 'with no auspicious voice I pray'.

picks.style: witch's incantation, bone flute and frame drum over drone, whisper rising to a keen, litany, hypnotic, accelerating
picks.why: The spell itself: garlands bound by nine serpents, Nessus' blood, Harpy feathers, the wings of the Stymphalian bird — an offering-list built as a chant.

picks.style: latin dramatic aria, storm-tossed strings and unstable harmony, torn female voice, alternating tender and violent, rubato
picks.why: 'Wrath drives out piety and piety wrath' — she holds her children, then lets them go: 'Wrath, where you lead, I follow.'

picks.style: english georgian air, chamber organ and viol, warm contralto, trochaic, serene, unhurried
picks.why: 'Give me then, in that Retreat, give me, O indulgent Fate' — the whole world handed away line by line in exchange for contemplation.

picks.style: restoration song, lute and theorbo, wry soprano, dance-like, biting, sighing at the turn
picks.why: Marked A SONG in the text: 'Vain Love, why do'st thou boast of Wings, that cannot help thee to retire!' — with a built-in closing couplet.

picks.style: storm ode, tremolo strings and low drum, dramatic soprano over unsettled harmony, gusting, awed
picks.why: Birds blown out of their nightly seats — 'your unentail'd, your undivided Air, where no Proprietor was ever known' — a whole politics inside a hurricane.

picks.style: english hymn, chamber organ and strings, plain tender tenor, common meter, slow, humane
picks.why: 'Aloud the speechless suppliant cries' — the newborn who cannot explain its own wants, and then 'That infant, Lord! am I.'

picks.style: benedicite litany, organ and brass with congregational chorus, rolling, oceanic, mounting praise
picks.why: 'Ye whales, that stir the boiling deep, or in its dark recesses sleep' — the Benedicite done as a roll-call, made to be sung antiphonally.

picks.style: classical hymn to apollo, harp and flutes, bright high voice, hushed then radiant, ceremonial
picks.why: 'Be still, ye vaulted skies! be still... He comes! his unshorn hair behind loose floating to the wanton wind' — silence commanded, then the god arriving.

picks.style: late latin mock-litany, plainchant with hand drum, sly male voice with chorus on the refrain, mock-solemn, building, comic
picks.why: 'Do not pull my verses to pieces' opening and closing a mock-prayer of saints, drowned barbarians and guests dying trying to out-drink the host.

picks.style: scots ballad, fiddle and small harp, warm male voice, lilting then wistful, with a called refrain
picks.why: Adam Smith 'curs'd with an unpoetic head' running straight into 'Busk ye, busk ye, my bonny, bonny bride' — a real Yarrow refrain to carry it.

picks.style: greek battle-chant, low drum and rasping strings, hard declamatory male voice, clipped, grim, unadorned
picks.why: Only candidate, but the point is made by the thing itself: three clauses stripped of conjunctions — a dagger, a bleeding foe, a corpse dragged.
